title: What is the Accenture Strategy interview process, and how should you prepare?
description: How Accenture's strategy and consulting roles tend to hire: HR screens, behavioural and case interviews with a technology angle, and a final senior…
hook: Accenture's strategy interviews usually combine a screening conversation, rounds that pair a case with behavioural questions, and a final round with more senior people. Cases are often less scripted than at MBB and tend to touch technology, so you need to show how a recommendation would actually be delivered, not just what it is. The exact steps vary by country, level and team.
body:
Where strategy sits at Accenture now

Accenture is best known for technology, but it also hires strategy and management consultants. In 2025 it brought strategy, consulting, Song (its creative and marketing arm), technology and operations together into one unit called Reinvention Services. In practice that means the role you apply for may not say "Accenture Strategy" in the title. Read the job description for the team, the level and the type of work, and prepare for that rather than for a label.

It also explains the flavour of the cases. Much of the firm's work joins a strategic question to a technology change, so interviewers want to hear that you can think about both.

What the process usually looks like

Candidate reports and Accenture's own advice point to a common shape, though the number of rounds differs by country and level:

  1. Screening conversation with a recruiter or consultant about your background and why Accenture.
  2. Interview rounds that pair a case with behavioural and situational questions ("What would you do if a client disagreed with your analysis?").
  3. A final round with more senior people, which can feel more like a discussion than a formal case.

Accenture's careers blog on case interviews notes that an interviewer may spend the first half asking about your experience or start with the case straight away. It advises asking what success means for the client, talking through your assumptions, using pen and paper, and paying attention to details the interviewer mentions, because they usually matter. Ask your recruiter whether your round includes a presentation or a technical discussion as well.

The technology angle, without being technical

Expect cases that touch digital channels, data, cloud, automation or AI. You do not need to code. You do need to explain what a technology changes for the business, in four plain terms: cost, customer experience, speed and risk. And you need to say how the change would land: who has to work differently, what has to be built, and how you would know it is working.

A worked example: automating customer service

Prompt: a retailer receives 500,000 routine customer enquiries a year, each costing $4 to handle. An automated assistant could resolve 60% of them at $0.50 each. Should it go ahead?

Step 1: size the headline saving

Today: 500,000 × $4 = $2.0M a year. With automation, 300,000 enquiries cost 300,000 × $0.50 = $150k and the other 200,000 still cost 200,000 × $4 = $800k. New total $950k, so the gross saving is $1.05M a year.

Step 2: take off what the headline ignores

Assume (illustratively) $200k a year to run and monitor the system, plus $500k one-off to build it. If 5% of the automated customers are not really helped and call back, that is 15,000 × $4 = $60k. Net yearly saving: $1.05M − $200k − $60k = $790k. Payback on the build: $500k ÷ $790k ≈ 0.63 years, about eight months.

Step 3: say how you would deliver it

Start with the two or three enquiry types the system handles most reliably, such as order tracking. Pilot with a share of traffic, track resolution rate, repeat contacts and customer satisfaction, and keep a clear route to a human. Train the service team for the harder enquiries they will now handle, and agree in advance what result would make you stop.

Weak: "AI can cut costs by 60%, so they should roll it out everywhere."
Strong: "The gross saving is about $1M a year, but after running costs and repeat contacts it is closer to $790k, with payback in under a year. I'd pilot it on order tracking first and only scale if repeat contacts stay below 5%."

The strong answer does the maths, questions its own headline and ends with a test. That is the habit Accenture interviewers are looking for. Our payback and NPV guide shows how to extend this kind of calculation.

Behavioural and situational questions

Prepare five or six stories with real detail: a time you led without authority, handled a difficult stakeholder, learned a new tool fast, and delivered under pressure. Situational questions ask what you would do; answer with a short plan and, if you can, a moment when you did something similar. Our guide to common fit questions lists what each one is testing.

For "Why Accenture?", link the firm's mix of strategy and delivery to something you have done. "I enjoy seeing a recommendation implemented, as I did when..." is far stronger than "Accenture is a global leader."

Common mistakes

  • Stopping at the strategy. Always add how it would be tested and delivered.
  • Hiding behind jargon. Say "the system answers order-tracking questions", not "leverage AI-driven omnichannel capabilities".
  • Ignoring the people side. A new system saves nothing if people keep working the old way. Mention training and ownership.

Practise now

1. A bank wants to move 40% of its 2 million yearly branch transactions to its app. Each branch transaction costs $3 and each app transaction $0.20. What is the yearly saving?

Show the answer

40% of 2 million is 800,000 transactions. Each saves $3 − $0.20 = $2.80, so 800,000 × $2.80 = $2.24M a year. Then ask what it costs to drive adoption, whether branches can actually shrink, and which customers would be left behind.

2. The client asks, "Why not roll the new system out everywhere at once?" What do you say?

Show the answer

"A pilot lets us check the saving is real and catch problems before every customer sees them. If the pilot hits its targets in eight weeks, we scale in waves, so the cost of waiting is small and the cost of a failed big launch is large."

Where to practise next

Build the core first with the complete guide to cost reduction cases, then add technology-flavoured cases from the PrepForCase casebook. Details here were checked in November 2026; always confirm the format with your recruiter.
